newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Chirac, Jospin stress respect.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac, Jospin stress respect.

text.p: Conservative President Jacques Chirac and Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin promised to work together to serve national interests at a cabinet meeting on Thursday launching a new bout of power-sharing in France.

"Here we are in a new period of 'cohabitation'," Chirac told the first meeting of Jospin's "Pink-Green-Red" cabinet that includes women in senior posts, Communists for a first time since 1984 and a Green minister of the environment.

"I do not doubt that it will take place in a dignified manner with mutual respect and a constant concern for France's interests," he told the 26-strong government seated around an oval table in the gilded Elysee Palace.
The new period of cohabitation was the third in the history of France's Fifth Republic, which began in 1958, but the first between a leftist prime minister and a rightist head of state.

Jospin, who led the left's upset victory over Chirac's centre-right allies in Sunday's National Assembly election, said the 30-minute cabinet talks launching power-sharing went "well, very well". He said the tone was serious but relaxed.

The Paris Bourse saluted a broadly pro-European government, in which Communists hostile to a European single currency were confined to the transport and sports ministries. The CAC-40 index was up almost three percent in early afternoon.
Chirac, who sat with a fixed smile when television cameras were briefly allowed in to film the meeting, stayed out of a cabinet photograph on the steps of the Elysee afterwards.

Jospin promised to respect Chirac's prerogatives under the 1958 constitution, which gives the president a big role in foreign policy and defence. The government focuses primarily on domestic policy, where the main challenge is record 12.8 percent unemployment.

Chirac gambled disastrously by calling the election 10 months ahead of schedule, hoping his centre-right allies would win re-election to give him five clear years of conservative rule until his own seven-year term expires in 2002.
Instead, he is the greatly diminished prisoner of a hostile majority and his own Gaullist party is in disarray following its election defeat.
After the cabinet meeting, Jospin, 59, left for a first official trip abroad, going to the Swedish city of Malmo for a gathering of Socialist heads of government and parties.
He will address the conference on Friday and hold talks with Britain's new Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair.
In the foreign policy realm, Jospin said he would attend a Franco-German summit in Poitiers, France, on June 13.

But in a sign of deference to Chirac, he would discuss participation at international summits with Chirac "in the interest of France and the state," said Olivier Shrameck, head of Jospin's private office.
Major international meetings this month include a European Union summit in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17, and a summit of the Group of Seven nations in the U.S. city of Denver on June 20-22.
French media generally praised Jospin's cabinet, which ditched most of the "elephants" from late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand's era.
"A government with a clean sweep," the conservative daily Le Figaro said with grudging admiration. "Good Luck!" the Communist daily L'Humanite said in a banner headline.
The smooth start contrasted with the start of the first cohabitation in 1986 when Mitterrand vetoed the choices of Chirac, who was prime minister, for defence and foreign affairs.

"I felt as if I was surrounded by men of whom 60 percent hate me and 80 percent are fighting me. I was alone this morning, very alone," Mitterrand said of his first cabinet session with Chirac. Mitterrand also shared power from 1993-95.
On the right, feuding intensified over the leadership of the Rally for the Republic party, founded by Chirac, with widening pressure for defeated prime minister Alain Juppe to stand down.
Former National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin, a favourite of the right to succeed Juppe, formally announced he was putting forward his candidacy for the leadership.

Seguin, a leader of the narrowly-defeated "no" campaign when French voters approved the Maastricht treaty on European union in a 1992 referendum, said he would also stand as interim parliamentary floor leader of the party.
